utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Baca, on Tuesday you concluded by telling us that you worked on a daily basis together with the UNESCO observers from end of November onwards. Did the institute, together with UNESCO observers, develop an action plan to organise damage assessment?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We did develop an action plan together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you set up damage assessment teams; and if so, what was their composition?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did set up teams, and we did distribute them throughout parts of town. We divided up the town for this to be easier, and the teams were made up, for the most part, of two individuals; one was an art historian and the other being an architect. So it was a two-man team, and it comprised all the different professional aspects.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many teams did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About eight. I can't tell you the exact number, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you develop a particular reporting system, and how was it different from what you did in October and November?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did develop a particular methodology, in fact, for registering and recording the damages at the proposal and in cooperation with the gentlemen from UNESCO. This differed from the previous reports that had been done and the reporting system because it was far more decisive. That is to say -- let me quote an example to illustrate this. We had the exact time, description of the damage, the day and date of the shelling, and the categorisation of the damages. This was very important because, as far as was possible at that time, this gave us a concrete evaluation of the damages incurred with the categories of the damages themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, attached to the proofing summaries we have actually submitted two sets of these reports. They do not need to be exhibited separately because they are actually part of the big report that we would like to tender under tab 16. But the witness could explain certain matters along these two reports. Can the witness have these two examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Baca, we have first the church of Sigurata, or monastery of Sigurata, and you have here the date of your inspection and the date of the incident, and there is actually a very precise time when this monastery was hit. Can you explain how you could be so sure about the time.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the simple reason that this information was supplied us by the nuns themselves from the monastery who, at the time of the shelling, were in the monastery and they were able to tell us the exact time. This, of course, wasn't what happened with all the lists that we filled in, but in this case it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This report actually is -- was done by yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I and my colleague Nikola, an architect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have listed here the type of projectiles, and you have given a very precise figure here. How could you do that? How were you able to distinguish between the calibres of the mortars?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the request and under the organisation of the representative of UNESCO, Mr. Bruno Carnez and Colin Kaiser, in our conservation department they organised a lecture for us with a professional, one professional, and that professional explained the four or five types of projectiles and how we could differentiate between them and recognise them. And how did we know exactly was your question. Well, sometimes we didn't. For example, there's one case here where we list three direct hits. We describe two, but the third projectile, we didn't know what kind it was, whereas the bullet parts would be found by some people and they would keep them, or we found them on the spot. So there were different types of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also -- in this report you mention direct hits, and in the next report we will discuss you also mentioned indirect hits. How could you distinguish between those two types?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, direct hits cause a great amount of damage, and it's quite clear when you look at it. Indirect hits are, for the most part, superficial damages which were caused by -- damages caused by parts of the projectile or shrapnel. So we were able to distinguish between them; the strength of the impact and the type of damage incurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And including -- included in this church of Sigurata little bundle, there is also a page showing mortar shells. Was that something you were explained when you had your training? I know it's a little bit further in this.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were examples that they showed us during our training sessions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this page with the various shells, that's actually part of tab 14. We come to this later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this same -- in this same document, we have also a few different additional pages, the last two, actually. They refer to 1992 shellings. Was that same church shelled also in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was shelled on the 29th of May, 1992. It was very serious damage to the roof construction of the church, and in fact, there's a large hole on -- in the very arch of the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this --

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vault.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This last page -- these two last pages, are these actually parts of a UNESCO report that was compiled later on?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is a report of the damages caused in 1992 in May and June, and it is a component part of the UNESCO report as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these two pages actually belong to tab 15, and we come to this document later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have also -- from this huge report, you have also picked the damage done to the Franciscan monastery. How many hits did this monastery get in October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-seven direct hits.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the report there is mention of where the monastery was hit. Was also, in addition to that, damage done to the interior; the furniture, and sculptures and those kind of things?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Damage was done to the interior, and the very valuable monastery library was affected and the very valuable furniture inside it. Damage was also done to the stone carvings dating back to the fourteenth and beginning of the fifteenth century, the decorative stonework and carvings of the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this report that actually consists of various separate sections related to sections in the building, you have also mentioned the damage, the severe damage to the balustrade. Why is that something to stress?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We laid emphasis on this because this type of architectural carvings are particularly difficult to reconstruct. So it was an original balustrade, original carvings, and the reconstruction of this would be highly complex because all the details have to be identical to the original, they have to be carved from the same type of stone, and of course they require the best possible professionals and artists, which means a serious undertaking, serious methodology, top-level professionals and cooperation among all the different professional profiles. That would be needed if we were to construct it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was your survey of the damage completed?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first report, the preliminary report on the damages up until June -- the 6th of December, 1991. And on the 6th of January was when it was actually completed, in 1992. So it began in December and was completed in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender this preliminary report. It's tab 16. And I will discuss a few matters in this report with the witness. It's actually three binders, and the first binder with the English version has a summary at the beginning and then actually the compilation of all these separate reports, building by building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it looks as though we will have to go into special training to be able to lift these binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will only deal with the witness with the first 12 pages. The rest is actually just the details that could be checked if one wanted to do that. Can the witness have the first -- just the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, on the first page - actually, it's page 2 in the English version - there are listed all the participants in the survey, and after a photo there is an introduction part where the cooperation with UNESCO representatives is discussed. You have already mentioned that, and we wouldn't have to repeat it. On page 6 in the English version, there is also the dates -- there are the methods applied and the dates of the shelling. You have already mentioned these dates to us. And on page 8 in the English version, there are the categories, listed the categories of damage. Is that a general worldwide category or was that something developed together with UNESCO for Dubrovnik itself?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is something that we developed together with UNESCO for Dubrovnik itself, that's right, this categorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these categories 1 to 4 we will also find in the damage reports for each building?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have also on that same page, you have the four basic types of damage that you always looked for and mention in the reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And following then are maps, and I would like to have these maps now put to you and on the ELMO. It's the map that's already actually tendered, and it's Exhibit 326, tab 25. It's the map where all the hits are indicated. Was this map developed by your institute?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We did develop the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And there are nine buildings indicated here as totally destroyed. Can you tell us what kind of buildings were totally destroyed? And you should, with the help -- with the pointer, with the help of the pointer point them out to us.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A total of nine damaged buildings, burnt. Two were residential facilities; 1 and 2. These are residential buildings. All the other buildings were, in fact, baroque palaces. The buildings which have just been outlined means that they were partially burnt buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'd like to remind you that this tab hasn't been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I was just reminded that it would be tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The other -- the other markings are the hits on other buildings. Yes. And then I would like to put to you another map, and it is actually Exhibit -- it would become Exhibit 326, tab 26. Can you explain this map to us: What -- who made the map and what do the different colours indicate?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map was made by our institute. The categories or, rather, the colours indicate the category of damage. Black stands for a completely burnt down building; the orange colour indicates serious constructive damage both to the roof and the walls; and the yellow indicates constructive damage of either the roof or the walls; and the green indicates non-constructive damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baca, could you tell me, is it everything, every building in the old Dubrovnik that was protected by UNESCO, not just some buildings, some parts? Am I right? Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right. Dubrovnik is protected as a whole and all the buildings within it, including the walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Baca, looking at actually the colour -- the maps with the various categories, it looks as if almost -- yes, the majority of the buildings were hit. Could you give us these general figures? How many buildings altogether were in these categories, in these four categories? Do you have the figures, the overall figures?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know those figures by heart. If the Court would permit, I would refer to a document, because I -- it is very difficult for me to give you the exact figures by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, if you've got a document there that can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The first category of burnt palaces, there was a total of nine. Serious damage, structural damage was suffered by 92 buildings. Structural damage was suffered by 218 buildings, and non-structural damage, 144 buildings. It should be noted that in the historical nucleus of the city there is a total of 824 buildings within the entire urban entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Baca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness brought this document that was provided by her institute, but we think it's enough to have just the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So from that, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we could make a deduction as to the percentage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you, by chance, have the percentages, Ms. Baca?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seventy per cent of the roofs were damaged. And as to the buildings, about 60 -- 55.6 per cent at that point in time. We're talking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about damage covered by the preliminary report and not the damage inflicted in 1992. That is not included.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the members of the UNESCO prepare a separate report related to that same period, that is November, December 1991, and are you aware of this report?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that such a report exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's tab 11, tab 11 of the Exhibit 408.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to this report, I would just like to refer to page 34 where actually you find that same figures that the witness just gave, the nine buildings burned, the 92 buildings serious structural damage, 218 buildings category 3, and 144 buildings category 4. And here you also have the percentages. You find them on page 34. And these -- these findings in the UNESCO reports, is that based on your cooperation?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are based on our cooperation, and the documentation that we had prepared was used for those reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on page 22 of this report, there is a mentioning of smoke being seen after shelling did happen. Are you aware whether any tyres were burned to produce an image of a burning town? Did you ever see something like this or hear anything like this?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of any such thing. Ships were set on fire, cars were hit by grenades and burnt, but I have no knowledge about tyres.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your institute, did it also assess damage to cultural property in other parts of Dubrovnik, and did you prepare reports of that kind? Other than the old town.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we completed the report on the historical nucleus of the town, we continued listing damage inflicted on cultural property throughout the territory of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the -- can the usher please put the city map to the witness, and it's -- this is a map that's already in evidence. It's Exhibit 326, tab 23, and it gives us the town -- the town in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And could you point out the regions where there were also cultural monuments that were hit and damaged. Just the regions and maybe briefly say what kind of buildings were damaged.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can point it out. There was Gruz. This part of the town where certain important buildings from the sixteenth and seventeenth century are situated, with an architecture that is typical of our area and that of Italy. These were holiday homes. Similar damage was inflicted again on two summer homes from the same period in this area and in the immediate vicinity of the old town. So this is something that needs to be pointed out, that extremely valuable buildings protected by law were also seriously damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the university library destroyed, do you know, or damaged?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was completely burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is exactly here. I am pointing it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing right from the park, between the park and the old town. Yes. Are you aware that the UNESCO observers also prepared a report mentioned -- entitled "Dubrovnik 1991-1992," including now the damage done in summer 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's tab 14. And in relation to this report, this report has on page 10 an explanation regarding the conventions. It's on page 13. Historical data. And there you also find on page 24 this page with the mortars mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And are you also familiar with a UNESCO report in relation to the damage now adding figures, costs of restoration? Are you aware of such a report?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is part of their report, both the costs of restoration and the 1992 damage and a plan or, rather, the order of priorities for the reconstruction. And in that respect, it differs from the -- our reports up until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's tab 15 of Exhibit 408.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You already mentioned, and it is also said here in this report, that the town was shelled in May, June 1992. What was ongoing in relation to the JNA or, rather, the VJ at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 26th of May the army started to withdraw from the western part of Dubrovnik, and also it withdrew from the immediate surroundings of the town. And three days later, after that withdrawal, on the 29th of May the historical nucleus of the town was shelled, then again on the 8th of June, and again on the 19th of June. So there were three shellings of the historical nucleus of the city after the withdrawal. This time, these were shells of greater strength because obviously the distance from which the shelling came was greater. So that the damage inflicted in that period was extremely grave. Very serious structural damage was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you review a video when you came here and we prepared your testimony, did you review a video related to the shelling of the 6th of December and the extent of the damage?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what you saw on the video, did that cover your own observations when you went through the town immediately after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there were fewer people, but the observation was the same. That day when I was coming into town, there were more people. There were -- the fire brigades were out. There were many people who were crying and people rushing to work. So it was far more crowded than shown on the picture, but the damage is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have put together five minutes that actually show the totally destroyed palaces and also the monastery that the witness referred to. We would like to show it, but if you think it's not time for doing so, we wouldn't insist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's five minutes, I think we might see that. It'll be five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. It's tab 19, and tab 19 is actually the entire video.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you may -- if you could assist us when you see it, just telling us which palace it is that is destroyed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the destroyed palace in the Siroka Street. The street is called Siroka or Brod. It is a baroque palace. This is the next burnt palace, also a baroque palace, in another street. It is known as the Martinusic palace. And we're in the same street known as Od Kuca Street. This is the St. Josef church. And right next to it is the next baroque palace that was burnt down. The Orthodox church in Dubrovnik. The cross on Mount Srdj that was shelled. Another palace, another baroque palace. This is the internal decorative plaster, the decorations over the doors, the gates, the cupboards, and the staircase as it used to be. Here you see the Franciscan monastery and the damage on the roof. The Minceta tower with the UNESCO flag on it. And again, this is the UNESCO flag and the damage to the roof below. The whole complex of the Franciscan monastery dates back to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Parts of it are even older. This is another direct hit in the very corner between the church and the rest of the monastery, a direct hit of the roof of a part of the monastery, and the damage to architectural plasterwork. This is a direct hit on the floor and the Gothic Renaissance balustrade that was completely destroyed. So it is very difficult to reconstruct it including all the details and using the same kind of stone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Baca, you have stated on the last page of your statement and in the last paragraph that you are a member of the HDZ since 1990. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, and that is my private affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying whether that is your private affair or not. I'm just referring to your membership in a political party which came into power in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you regularly attend HDZ meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was not an active member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you. You were not an active -- no. You said that you were not an official.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope a member is an active member by being a member. But tell me, please, do you know when your party started the preparations and plans for the activities, the military activities, in connection with Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no information about that. Anyway, that is not the subject of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The subject of your testimony is certainly your statement, Ms. Baca. So please bear that in mind. And I'm asking you questions within that context as well as about what you told us a moment ago. On page 2 of your statement, in paragraph 6, you say that tension increased in 1991 -- "As the tension increased in 1991, I increasingly feared that the JNA would attack Dubrovnik." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you start to fear that the JNA would attack Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we saw what was going on throughout Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the time when the JNA barracks were blocked all over Croatia? Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the month of August 1991, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the basis for your fears? Why did you think that the JNA would attack Dubrovnik? You said you're talking about the month of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is causing this? Yes. We'll try again. Can we find what the trouble is that's making this noise. It's quite impossible to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I would like to emphasise the paragraph numbers should be numbered in the same way. I note that this is para number 5 in English, and the accused referred to number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is everything all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The problem which the usher is sorting out has to do with your headset which you won't wear. But we'll put it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's nothing unusual today in relation to any other day, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There obviously is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There obviously is because of this interference which is coming over. But let's see how we come along. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In just in relation to Judge Kwon's question, actually it is the same numbering and the accused has misspoken. It's paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I answer the question? I heard it in spite of the noise. May I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the reports of the Ministry of Culture that were sent to us spoke of certain damage already done in the north of Croatia to cultural property covered by The Hague convention. And the activities and the order that arrived from the Ministry of Culture prompted us to start to mark cultural property under The Hague Convention, and it became clear to me then what could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are claiming -- and let me not give the wrong number of the paragraph again. You're claiming on the second page, 2, that the director of the institute at the time, Dora Valjalo-Kondres, in July and August 1991 called you and your colleagues back from annual leave for you to protect the most important historical monuments in and around Dubrovnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in July and August, you're called back from your holiday to protect the monuments in Dubrovnik and its environs. Now, why, please tell me, you put up scaffolding, wooden planks and so on when in those months no one was attacking, not Dubrovnik but even the surroundings nor in that area was there any kind of intimation of any conflicts breaking out?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the order came from the Ministry of Culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So an order arrived.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And secondly, I already said that the situation in other parts of Croatia had in fact prompted such an order to be issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know, Ms. Baca, that in the area of Dubrovnik over the last 20-year period, there were no military personnel except, of course, for the holiday homes for them which were not any sources that could provoke any fears or apprehensions.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but the question is: Why was Dubrovnik attacked at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then: You're a local from Dubrovnik, you're familiar with all the people there, at least those in leading positions; does the name Martin Vukorep mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was head of the staff of the Territorial Defence of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dubrovnik, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name; I don't know his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You know the name but you don't know exactly what position he held. You don't know that he was chief of the Territorial Defence in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you necessarily had to know that. I'm just asking you whether you knew that.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. July 1991 was certainly not a month in which there were any intimations of any kind of an attack on Dubrovnik. Isn't that right, Ms. Baca?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, there were no such intimations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you then please read out, aloud, what that gentleman, Mr. Vukorep, says in a letter he sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia personally to Minister Simo Djodan, and in person to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this witness going to know about what this man sent to the Ministry of Defence? This witness has come here to talk about the damage. You want to read something out which is totally irrelevant to her evidence. Now, move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. It is highly relevant for the testimony, the fact that in July, the month of July, there was absolutely no danger from the Yugoslav People's Army in the surrounding parts of Dubrovnik in any way whatsoever. And it is quite obvious, if we look at the statement by this witness, that in July and August, preparations were already under way to fortify those buildings, to build up protective barriers and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Milosevic, we all know your case. What you can ask the witness is what she saw. You can ask her that, of course, whether she saw any preparations for war, whether there was any building in the old town, whether there were guns moved in. Of course you can ask questions like that if that's your case. What she saw and heard herself, you can ask her that. What you can't ask her about is some letters passing between third parties about which she'll know absolutely nothing. If you want put the evidence before us, I've said it many times, you can do so when it's your turn to give evidence and put evidence before us. But you can't waste time asking this witness about things about which she knows nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think that my question was a pertinent one and that as its foundations we have the fact that the witness explained that there were no military forces in Dubrovnik, and that is why, following on from that statement of hers. Because she was asked in fact by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff about this, I assume that I too have the right to ask my question during the cross-examination. So could we have your comments, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you cannot do is put a letter passing between two third parties to her. If there is something concrete in the letter that you want to put, then you can put it. Did you see forces being moved in? Something of that sort. Did you see armament in the Hotel Excelsior, or whatever it is. You can put that. But you can't put this letter to her and try and get her to read it out. It's an abuse of the process. Now, move on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine, Mr. May. I really don't wish to abuse the witness in any way or impose letter-reading on her. But on the 23rd of June, 1991, the Chief of Staff says that reviewing the overall situation within the Dubrovnik defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can tell us about it. At the moment, you're asking this witness questions. You can tell us all about it when you come to give your evidence, but for the moment, you're confined to asking this witness questions. Now, if you've got no other questions to ask her, we will let her go rather than detaining her and wasting everybody's time. Now, I've told you can't read out the letter to her or get her to read it out. Now, move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, please. Can we get one thing clear? It says here that the man is tendering his resignation because he doesn't want to be at the beck and call on the 116th Guards Corps of Dubrovnik, which means that in June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, I'm going to now consult with my colleagues as to whether we should stop this. You're not paying attention to the rulings. The ruling is very simple: You cannot put this letter about somebody else to her. She's nothing to do with the guards division or anything like that. Now, either you move on or I stop the cross-examination. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Baca, do you know that at that time, that is to say already in June, in Dubrovnik there was a brigade of the Croatian National Guards Corps in place?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I'm an art historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. You don't know anything about that. Fine. But you do know, and we've seen that here, we were shown a big binder full of documents, UNESCO documents, which by the way, that same SFRY drew up with UNESCO quite a number of years beforehand, where Mrs. Retzlaff quoted in particular the positions taken by The Hague Convention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I resume, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, we have seen here many documents. Mrs. Retzlaff quoted in particular The Hague Convention provisions which relate to the protection of localities and the obligation to refrain from any use of localities for military purposes. Therefore, Mrs. Baca, on the one hand you have the presence of the Croatian National Guards Corps, which was treated in Yugoslavia as a paramilitary formation at that time. It was in Dubrovnik. And to such an intensity that the organs of Dubrovnik reacted themselves. On the other hand, you were ordered to fortify and protect the town. So Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fortify? To fortify the town? That wasn't the witness's evidence. They were simply -- or are you suggesting she was fortifying it in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I meant was to protect the buildings in the town in preparation, quite obviously, for some expected combat that nobody could have known about in the month of June. So that's what I'm pointing to here, Mr. May. I am pointing out the obvious preparations that went on to protect -- to use Dubrovnik as a protected town for provocations, because in June, July, and August, there was absolutely no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll put that to the witness. As far as she knows, she can deal with that. From what you saw and from the work that you were doing marking the buildings and the like, did it appear to you that the town was being prepared for a provocation? Did it ever occur to you that that -- or did anybody say, "This is the plan," something of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never. And as far as the applications of The Hague Convention are concerned, if you read it carefully - and I'm sure that you know this - that the preparations for the protection of cultural heritage is conducted during peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What did you think you were doing? What did you think the purpose of what you were doing, marking the buildings, was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose of it was to prevent damage to cultural sites, or to prevent them from being used for military purposes, in conformity with the provisions of The Hague Convention, to the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just to clear this matter up. I don't mind if you're going to give me a yes or no answer, all I wish is to get an answer from you. Do you consider that it is not contested in view of the -- your activities to protect the monuments and in view of the presence of the 116th Brigade of the Croatian National Guards Corps and the activities of the TO of Dubrovnik, that the Croatian authorities already in June, July, and August 1991 were preparing themselves from something -- for something in the military sense? Is that quite obvious or not?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in my field of expertise and competence to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then just give me a brief answer. In July or August of that year, was any attack launched on Dubrovnik and its environs?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any attack taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So despite the fact that nobody was actually attacking Dubrovnik and that in its vicinity in July there was no fighting going on, you and the Dubrovnik authorities were taking steps which intimate the advent of shelling of the town and conflicts in the old town proper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. We were acting according to instructions and in keeping with the Ministry of Culture. Our Institute for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, in keeping with the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Croatia, working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't doubt that you were given instructions by the Ministry of Culture, and rest assured, Mrs. Baca, that I don't consider you yourself to be a participant in any of these events at all, the ones that I'm talking about and referring to. But with respect to your testimony, one can draw certain conclusions. Have you heard of the name of Ivan Varenina at all?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I won't ask you anything about him in that case. Just tell me this: You spent your whole life in Dubrovnik, since you were born almost. Do you know that that man is a local from Dubrovnik? Have you heard of him at all?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't heard of him. I just don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. But you did know the townsfolk of Dubrovnik, people who were natives of Dubrovnik, born there, practically all of them.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say I knew all of them. I can't know everybody in town. Maybe I knew them by sight, but to know somebody closer, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought Dubrovnik was a small town and people born in Dubrovnik would know each other. But anyway, on page 2, paragraph 7, you say that you spent your working days in Dubrovnik. "I was living during the working week in Dubrovnik and spent the weekends at Cavtat with my parents and my sister." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So during the time of preparation for this alleged defence of Dubrovnik, you went to Cavtat for your weekends unimpeded, and you went to and from Dubrovnik and Cavtat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's Croatian territory. Why should I be impeded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not questioning, Mrs. Baca, that Dubrovnik and Cavtat are in the territory of Croatia. All I'm saying is that during the time these preparations went on to defend and protect Dubrovnik, you were nevertheless free to travel from Dubrovnik to Cavtat and back. So does that mean and is it true that during those preparations for this alleged defence, neither in Dubrovnik or in Cavtat - which is how many kilometres in the southerly direction from Dubrovnik? - or around those two towns either or on the road between the two towns, there was no JNA presence at all. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Dubrovnik was preparing for its defence; right? So tell me where the office is, the headquarters of your institute. Where were they in the old town?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right next to the Dominican monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. On page 2, paragraph 8, you say that: "Shortly after 8.00 a.m. on the 1st of October, the shelling commenced." Right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that nothing came before this, happened before this? Just quite suddenly somebody started shelling the town? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what events took place before that. I don't know what the forerunner was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But then, out of the blue, somebody started shelling the town. Is that it? Was that your impression?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And then you go on to say that on that same day - and there's a correction here - you say around noon, that is to say before the expulsion -- your office hours were over, you were allowed to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the town started to be shelled at 8.00 a.m., you stayed on the job at your workplace, and then sometime around noon you were allowed to leave the premises. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So despite the shelling, you spent more than half your working day at the institute in your offices; right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our offices were on the ground floor, and that's where we were. We took refuge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't spend that morning working at your workplace, but you went to a shelter of some kind, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of our office premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the building that we otherwise worked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you spend the time in your own office, working in your own office?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the time, yes; part of the time not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the intensity of the attack. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If it was an all-out attack, why didn't you leave your workplace? Because you weren't in the health service or the fire brigade or anything of that kind, and you have your own family, wouldn't it have been logical to have left your workplace, left your job and gone home because you were perhaps worried and anxious about your family members, your household, your relatives? Why didn't you leave your workplace before that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a director. She -- it was a lady, and she decided who was to stay, who was to leave, when we could stay, and when we could leave. We had our work obligations to fulfil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did she let you go home at noon?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that up until then she prevented you from leaving your institute?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody even asked to leave, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say you went to your uncle's apartment when you left. And as you noticed planes shelling Srdj at the time, military planes selling Srdj. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that the shelling began at 8.00 a.m., and after 12.00, when you went to your uncle's apartment, this was probably 2.00 or 3.00 p.m., and you saw that air force planes were shelling Srdj. What had been shelled before that? What was shelled?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Everything all around. We could see smoke. I don't know actually what was shelled. The historical nucleus of the town was not at that time, that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you; what did you say?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The historical nucleus of the town was not shelled at that particular time. It was Mount Srdj that was shelled from the planes, but what happened otherwise, I don't know. We saw smoke around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear that somebody opened fire from Dubrovnik, with respect to what you said when you said that the old town was not shelled but what was shelled was something else? This something else that was shelled, were those the positions occupied by the members of the National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that. I'm not a military expert, and I don't have any knowledge about this. I'm an art historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that the old town was shelled for the first time on the 23rd and 24th of October. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this happened on the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for those 23 days, you knew nothing at all about any kind of actions taken by these units from Dubrovnik against the JNA positions, before that period of 23 days or during that 23-day period?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on that day, according to your statement, quite a lot was damaged. Quite a number of buildings were damaged. That's what you say, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you've listed the buildings that were damaged. We've now seen the videotape of one building. And tell me, what was the damage on the other buildings?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've provided all my reports with the categories of damage, the number of buildings damaged and all the other details contained in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But on that day, you prepared just a brief report on the damage and an evaluation of the damage and sent it to Zagreb, to the Ministry of Culture; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you prepared a more thorough estimate of the damage after the 7th of December that same year?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when exactly did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 7th of December 1991 up until -- if you're talking about the details and if you're thinking of the damage after the 23rd and 24th of October, then we prepared that report the very next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Dubrovnik was actually heavily shelled on the 6th of December, 1991. No. It's not what you say, but several other witnesses have told us that. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, after this heavier shelling of Dubrovnik that occurred on the 6th of December, could you carry out a thorough evaluation of the damage in the old town that occurred on the 23rd and 24th of October, a month and a half prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we had taken note of all the damage made. And secondly, we prepared for each building an estimate. The buildings were not abandoned; people were living inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you or your institute have any video documents of the damage that was done on the 23rd and 24th of October?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are photo documents, not video documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you prepare a videotape?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have a video camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see that for this other side or -- you did have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the video camera -- do you know where the film came from on the 6th of December? Perhaps Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff can help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the film was not provided by the institute. It's actually the film provided by a witness that we will talk about later on, and the witness just reviewed it and confirmed that it's what she saw herself. It's from another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember the 11th of November, 1991? Was this a date that sticks in your memory for any reason at all?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 8th to the 13th of November, Dubrovnik was shelled. For five consecutive days there was an exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that members of the National Guards Corps from Dubrovnik - I suppose you will remember that because you were in Dubrovnik then - on the 11th of November managed to hit an ammunition depot of the JNA at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that. I have no knowledge about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this was quite a loud explosion, and you know nothing about it. We watched a videotape of an English reporter on which he says they have hit the warehouse, and then as a result of the explosion, the shells, fragments scattered over the old town. Don't you think that the damage on the roof of the Franciscan monastery, for instance, on the tiles of the roof, don't really appear to be direct hits but possible damage caused by fragments of shells after the ammunition depot was hit? Because if that had been a direct hit, then surely there should a crater or larger damage within the monastery itself as a result. Do you know anything at all about the damage caused as a result of the fragmentation of shells that hit the ammunition depot, fired by the National Guards Corps, and the resulting explosion?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can assert is that our list of damage, our preliminary reports, are extremely accurate and reliable. As for this, I have no idea about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I see that you don't wish to know anything about these things, though I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not a proper comment. The witness says she doesn't know. She doesn't know the cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She don't know about something that was so loud and spectacular that every citizen of Dubrovnik must have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, please, do you have any report about damage done on the 11th of November? Do you have that report?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the historical nucleus of the town, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the damage done on the 11th of November on those historical buildings? Could you tell us, briefly?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the same as on the 6th of December, only of less scope, lesser scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when these numerous shells went off and scattered all over Dubrovnik, the damage was of a lower intensity than on other days. Are you claiming that according to your reports, on the 11th of November the damage was lesser than on the other days?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm claiming exactly what is contained in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say in your report for the 11th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't cover just one date but the period from the 8th to the 13th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, do you claim that on that day the damage was less?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say on that day. I said during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So between the 8th and the 13th of November, the damage done to Dubrovnik was of the least intensity. Please tell me, did you then say that from the 8th to the 13th, which is the period to which your report refers, the damage done to Dubrovnik was least?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what then did you say? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said, and I am repeating, is that the first attack on the historical nucleus of the town of Dubrovnik occurred on the 23rd and the 24th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We established that.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second attack was from the 8th to the 13th of November, 1992, and the third on the 6th of December. Every following one was of greater intensity. The attack on the 23rd and the 24th of October was of the lowest intensity, as can be confirmed by the documentation, as can everything else, the documentation prepared by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the intensity was considerable at the time when this warehouse of ammunition was blown up. That is the period from the 8th to the 13th of November. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said everything I know about the damage and everything that is written about the damage in the period from the 8th to the 13th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come to adjourn. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got 20 minutes more, Mr. Milosevic, if you want it, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the investigators, Ms. Baca, that it seemed to you when speaking about the 6th of December, when you say that the shelling was intensive, that it seemed to you that most of the shells were falling on the old town or its immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what you assumed is something that you also heard on the radio.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me why, in spite of such heavy shelling, you spent the whole day in town. Why didn't you seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply we found the safest places within our own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, about 1.00 p.m., as you say, you were standing in front of the town and you saw somebody shelling Srdj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was shelling Srdj?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you heard several explosions in Lapad and saw shells coming from Lapad hitting Srdj?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in my statement was my personal impression, and I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that that is your personal impression. You say on page 4 that Srdj was being shelled and that it was being shelled from around Lapad. Did the JNA have any positions at Lapad in those days?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't think it did. Well, who had positions at Lapad?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that forces of the ZNG had positions at Lapad? You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Lapad is in Dubrovnik, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you record by video the damage done to buildings in the old town on the 6th of December? Because you say that that was the fiercest attack. Did you record that by video?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conservation department in Dubrovnik doesn't have a video camera, but we corroborated everything with photo documents, and we have those photographs in our department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when was the damage repaired?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The damage is being repaired to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any video document about the reconstruction and the repairs to that damage? As you say, this is going on to the present day. Do you have videotapes of that?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have photo documents, I must repeat. We still don't have a video recorder. But all other relevant documents do exist in the conservation department, such as photographs of the sites, exploratory work, architectural documents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the damage still recognisable on all the buildings that you mention in your written reports? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were documented. In some cases, they're not recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So in some cases they're not recognisable. You certainly know Zvonimir Franic.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he, too, was going to testify about the destruction you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to look at his report. He was director of your institute, wasn't he, for a brief time?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is what it said in his CV.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never director of the conservation department in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to look at his report and photographs of damage, for instance, on the chapel of Navjestenje, the Chapel of the Annunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Show us the photographs that you want the witness to see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please give her this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now show me, please, the damage that he refers to in his report on this chapel.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be described in an accompanying document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't answer what's in somebody else's report unless she's seen it. Perhaps, Mr. Milosevic, you'd tell us what the point of the question is. What is it you want dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are photographs that were produced here as evidence of the damage in Dubrovnik, and that is the same chapel, the Benedictine monastery, the Benedictine nunnery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And here you have those two photographs as well. This is the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Culture and Natural Heritage in Dubrovnik, and I'm asking the witness where the damage is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. It may be very difficult to see on a photograph of this sort which is of poor quality. It's a photocopy. If there is some point arising, there is another report which shows that buildings weren't damaged, it may well be that we can get that admitted in some other way. It's very difficult for the witness to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no separate report of Mr. Franic, to our knowledge, because Mr. Franic was part of the team that documented this huge report that we have now exhibited, and this is probably one building, a report referring to one separate building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused is entitled to ask about it. It sounds as though, Mr. Milosevic, it's the same report. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it may be that you could help since it was your witness who produced this. Can you tell us where this is likely to have come from?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are trying to find that separate little report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it was attached to the statement of Zvonimir Franic, who was here on the list of witnesses and was replaced by this witness. Will you look at these photographs as well. They have all been marked by the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with it in this way: We will find out which the report is. You've referred to this as a chapel. Now, tell us what the other two photographs that you're wanting the witness to look at are, and we'll put them in front of the witness. It will be very difficult for her, but we may ask her if she can see any damage or not, if that's the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. I have here several photographs. Mr. Franic signed this report on the 10th of July, 2000. That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please look at the photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Hand them back. Mr. Milosevic, will you tell us, for the record, what the photographs are of, please, the buildings, so we've got it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On one is the Benedictine monastery, the western wing or facade, probably, because it's not legible. And then the easterly facade. So it has been photographed from all sides. And in his report, he speaks of damages, and these are the photographs that he attaches to indicate this. So I wish to ask the witness to indicate where the damages on these buildings are because she worked with these buildings in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can hand that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will put them to the witness. The witness can have a look, and if she can see any damage, she can point it out, or if not, we can look at the report. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could get the ERN number on top of the document, we could easily find it, but without it's very hard to pick a photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see it first and then it can go to the Prosecution. Now, Ms. Baca, can you see any damage or not? That's really the point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is that these are very poor quality copies and that it's very difficult for me to see anything on them. Not only the damage but everything else is indistinct. As for the first photograph, on that I can notice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can point to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- damages along this part here, along the roof structure, by the absidia and the roof structure. That's where the damage lies, and you can see the difference compared to the rest of the walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us -- before we lose that one, the chapel, which chapel was it? It's got a name on it but it's not on the ELMO. Could you tell us, please, Ms. Baca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chapel is Navjestenje. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have it for the record. If you'd like to look at the other photographs to see whether you can see anything or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've already said these are very poor quality photocopies, and it's very difficult for me to see the facade and the damages and the windows. There are some white blemishes here. I can't say with any certainty what they are, but let me repeat that along with these photographs, there must be an accompanying text which locates the damages that are talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to look at the other photograph too. Then we'll get them handed to the Prosecution. Is there anything you can see on that you want to point out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see that here. All I can see is a white space here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what they mean, these white spaces or empty areas. I can't say either way, one way or the other, unless I have the documents attached to it and everything necessary for a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Baca, don't worry. We will get the report out, and we can look at that. But the accused is entitled to put these matters to you. Would you hand them to the Prosecution and then we'll identify where the report is. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if you'd let us know in due course where it is. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that you are bearing in mind the fact that I received those documents with Mr. Franic's statement from the other side over there. So the quality of the photographs and all the rest of it is something that they must be responsible for. But quite obviously you can see that we -- damages cannot be ascertained on those copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know when the photographs were taken? Perhaps you know that.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When normally were the photographs taken? Can you tell us generally how you went about photographing them? Did you do it at the same time as you made the report?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly it was done at the same time, but as there were eight different teams working simultaneously to register and record the war damages, sometimes what would happen was that a plan of the damages would be handed over to a photographer, and then he might take the photographs subsequently, afterwards, on the basis of the plan, because it wasn't -- it wasn't possible for the photographers to go around with each of the teams. Sometimes the photographs would be taken by the representatives of UNESCO, Colin Kaiser and Bruno Carnez, actually. They had their own cameras so they sometimes took the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of your statement, Mrs. Baca, you make mention of a report in the compiling of which you took part, and you say you signed it too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you attached those documents here for us to see?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the reports or, rather, the buildings that I dealt with are within the general documents handed over to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 8, you say that the report represents a copy of the authentic original reports.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, when did these come into being, these copied-out reports?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning. As soon as we got to work we would start making lists of the damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you something else.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to finish my answer? We would go back to our conservation department and then would write this out again or, rather, type then out on ordinary mechanical typewriters - we had no electricity - and then these forms were handed over to our director, the lady, and she would in turn hand them over to the gentlemen from UNESCO who would enter it into their joint collective documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say that this represents the exact copy of the source documents, tell me, please, where the source documents are, the original documents.

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source documents are in our documentary files. But as I say, everything was copied out the moment it was done, half an hour afterwards or an hour later, as soon as we arrived back in our offices in the conservation department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who authenticated and certificated the copies to say that they were true to the original?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were certified by Bruno and Colin, the UNESCO representatives. They were also certified by our director and two other colleagues who were in charge of the documents, Mr. Matko Betma, and Mrs. Bozena Popic, that is to say the team that coordinated and dovetailed all the material. If anything was left unclear, then this would be checked out and a final version made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You will remember the damages that you describe in your own report as you are the author of that report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 13 years have gone by since that time, but yes, I do confirm the truthfulness of my written word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, for example, were there any damages in the old town from Siroka Street to the Church of Saint Blaise? Can you tell us-- can you tell us, please, the Saint Blaise church -- from Siroka Street to Saint Blaise church, what were the damages?

utterances.speaker: ZANA BACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the facade was damaged as well as the eastern balustrade, the eastern part of the balustrade, by direct hit and that the eastern relief carvings and decorations were damaged, underneath the eastern window or on the window which bore The Hague Convention mark. And I don't know how many other direct hits to the roof structure. So all that has been recorded in diagram and in description of that, but I don't want to make any mistakes as to the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you told us that they -- you attended a short ballistics course of some kind. How were such minor damages able to be incurred by direct hits?
